title: Why Have Indonesia’s Fires Gotten So Bad?
gist: Indonesia may be on track for its worst-ever fire year — nearly 900,000 hectares burned January-August — driven by plantation agriculture, a severe El Niño and a disaster-agency budget slashed by roughly 90 percent. The brief also covers a Philippine Senate rule change that makes Sara Duterte's conviction (and exclusion from the 2028 race) more likely, and Bangkok floods with initial damages of 12.3 billion baht.

insights.claim: Nearly 900,000 hectares of Indonesian land burned from January to August 2026 according to Nusantara Atlas satellite data, more than by August 2019, the worst year in that organization's records; the fire season is expected to run until November.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Transboundary haze already reaching Singapore, Kuala Lumpur and Manila signals regional health, aviation and productivity disruption into Q4.

insights.claim: Plantation agriculture is the fundamental underlying cause of Indonesia's catastrophic fires: fire hotspots overlap almost perfectly with plantation density, as land clearing creates fuel, peatland drainage creates tinderboxes and fire is used to clear land.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Palm oil and pulp plantation operators face recurring regulatory, reputational and ESG risk each dry season.
insights.quote: Plantation agriculture is the fundamental underlying cause of the catastrophic forest fires of modern days.

insights.claim: El Niño is the biggest driver of year-to-year variation in Indonesian fire size: research found a one-degree Celsius rise in the central Pacific sea surface temperature anomaly corresponded to a 50 percent increase in hotspot detections in rural districts.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: El Niño forecasts can serve as a leading indicator for Southeast Asian haze, crop and commodity disruptions.
insights.quote: A one-degree Celsius increase in the sea surface temperature anomaly in the central Pacific corresponded with a 50 percent increase in hotspot detections in rural Indonesian districts.

insights.claim: Indonesia's disaster management agency BNPB had its budget slashed to 491 billion rupiah (about $27 million) this year from nearly 5 trillion rupiah in 2024, as the government cut programs to fund expansive social welfare policies.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Prabowo-era fiscal reprioritization toward welfare is weakening state capacity in areas like disaster response — a governance risk for investors.

insights.so_what: Promised crackdowns may prove limited where the state itself is a plantation stakeholder.

insights.claim: The Philippine Senate voted to require only two-thirds of senators attending the trial, rather than two-thirds of all senators, to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, making conviction much more likely and potentially barring her from the 2028 presidential race despite her poll lead.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Removes the frontrunner from the 2028 race, reshaping the Philippines' political and foreign-policy trajectory (including on China).

insights.claim: Several pro-Duterte senators cannot attend the trial — one is fleeing the International Criminal Court, two are arrested on corruption charges, one is on medical leave — so now just one Duterte-camp senator needs to flip, with six more under investigation.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Legal pressure on Duterte allies is translating directly into vote math against the dynasty.
insights.quote: Now, just one senator in the Duterte camp needs to flip.

insights.claim: Bangkok was declared a disaster zone with 10,000 troops deployed after 12.6 inches of rain fell from Thursday — nearly the city's usual total for all of September; initial damage estimates are 12.3 billion baht (about $366 million), with 2 billion baht allocated for relief.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Flood damage and supply panic-buying will weigh on Thai Q3/Q4 activity and fiscal space.

insights.claim: September floods across Thailand displaced 1.7 million people outside Bangkok and killed at least 23; for context, the November 2011 floods inundated nearly 10 percent of the country, affected 13 million people and caused an estimated $46.5 billion in damages.
insights.speaker: Joseph Rachman
insights.so_what: Thailand's recurring flood risk to its industrial base (cf. 2011 supply-chain shock) remains a material climate exposure.

insights.so_what: Structural flood vulnerability of the capital is a long-run climate risk for Thai real estate and infrastructure.
